name: Kente weaving at Bonwire and among the Ewe
subtitle: Kente is a strip-woven cloth made by Asante and Ewe weavers in Ghana.

facts.label: Where
facts.value: Bonwire is a town in the Ashanti region known specifically for Asante kente weaving.

facts.label: Who weaves
facts.value: Traditionally Asante and Ewe men weave kente, using a wooden treadle loom to make long strips.

facts.label: Who weaves in Bonwire
facts.value: In Bonwire women predominantly work in farming and men in weaving.

facts.label: How it is made
facts.value: Kente strips are woven on a double heddle loom that can be 200 feet or longer.

facts.label: Learning the craft
facts.value: Males born and raised in Bonwire are trained to weave kente.

facts.label: Size of the village
facts.value: In 1998 Bonwire had roughly 9,000 people, and the authors give a present figure close to 12,000.

facts.label: Origin story
facts.value: Bonwire's origin story names two farmer brothers, Kuragu and Ameyaw, as the first to weave kente in the 17th century.

facts.label: Ewe kente
facts.value: Ewe weavers are known for a popular version of kente called Agomevor, which dates to the sixteenth century.

facts.label: Ewe and Asante differences
facts.value: Ewe kente often shows a tweed effect from plying different coloured threads, and may include pictorial symbols.

facts.label: Museum
facts.value: The Bonwire Kente Museum is an initiative of the Ministry of Tourism, Arts and Culture and sits beside the Bonwire Kente Village, the hub for weaving and sales.

facts.label: Change and risk
facts.value: The chief of Bonwire asked government to help set up a factory for the yarn and raw materials of kente weaving, which are sometimes difficult to come by.

facts.label: Women's role
facts.value: Women play other roles in the kente economy with significant economic power, such as marketing and retailing.

parts.text: Kente is a strip-woven cloth made by Asante and Ewe weavers in Ghana. Bonwire, a town in the Ashanti region, is known for Asante kente weaving, where men weave on a double heddle loom and women mostly farm; Ewe weavers make their own version, known as Agomevor. A kente museum opened at Bonwire in 2024.
